Aasiaat (port locode GLJEG) is a town in western Greenland (Aasiaat Archipelago) located at Disko Bay's southern end. By population (around 3,000) it is Greenland's 5th-largest town. Its name means "Spiders" in Greenlandic.

Sometimes, Aasiaat is referred to as "the Town of the Whales", because marine mammals such as seals and whales are a common sight.

Aasiaat is a ferry port for Arctic Umiaq Line (freight and passenger shipping company). Arctic Umiaq serves the south-western Greenland route roundtrip from Nuuk.

Aasiaat is a compact Greenlandic town on the southern edge of Disko Bay, surrounded by a low archipelago of islands, channels and open water. For cruise visitors, the main attractions are the historic waterfront, Aasiaat Museum, local art and short boat trips into the archipelago. Most central sightseeing is straightforward on foot.

At a Glance

  • Independent sightseeing: Easy independently in the town centre.
  • Port access: Cruise passengers should normally expect to come ashore by tender. The local city map identifies a tourist pontoon and ferry landing in the central harbour area, but the exact landing point can vary by call.
  • Town centre: Immediately around the harbour, with most principal sights within a short walk.
  • Terrain: Roads through town are mostly paved or hard-surfaced, but there are slopes, uneven sections and exposed walking conditions.
  • Best for: A self-guided town walk, museum and art, harbour scenery, or a pre-arranged sea safari.

Getting from the Cruise Port

Aasiaat has a working commercial and ferry harbour rather than a purpose-built cruise terminal. Cruise ships may anchor offshore and tender passengers into the harbour. Follow the ship's instructions for the exact landing point and final tender time, as arrangements can change with the vessel and conditions.

Once ashore, walking is the most practical way to explore. The museum, church, old colonial buildings, shops and other central sights are clustered around the harbour. Taxis exist, but they are generally unnecessary for a normal town visit.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Explore the Historic Harbour and Aasiaat Museum

Allow: about 1.5–2 hours.

This is the simplest choice for a short port call. Walk through the harbour and preserved colonial area to Aasiaat Museum, housed in the former colonial manager's residence. The collections concentrate on local and Greenlandic history, including hunting, kayaking, sledding and traditional life.

The nearby sod house, historic waterfront buildings and Aasiaat Church make this a compact cultural circuit. Museum access and opening times should be checked on the day of the visit.

Follow Aasiaat's Art Around Town

Allow: about 1.5–2.5 hours.

Aasiaat has an unusually strong collection of public art for a town of its size. Murals decorate several apartment blocks, while stone sculptures by local artist Jens Erik Kjeldsen are scattered through the town. The assembly house also contains a large group of paintings created by Danish artist Per Kirkeby.

Destination Disko Bay publishes an Art'n'Walk self-guided route and a separate guide to Aasiaat's historic houses. These are useful additions to a cruise-day walk because the sights are dispersed through the central streets rather than concentrated in a single attraction.

Take a Sea Safari through the Aasiaat Archipelago

Allow: around 2 hours for a typical local boat excursion, plus time to reach the departure point and return to the tender.

The surrounding archipelago is one of Aasiaat's main attractions. Local boat trips may combine island scenery, icebergs and the historic whale graveyard, with the possibility of seeing whales. Summer is the main whale-watching season, although wildlife sightings are never guaranteed.

Organized excursion recommended: Boat departures are weather-dependent and may not align with a short cruise call. A cruise-line excursion or a locally pre-booked trip specifically timed around the ship is safer than trying to arrange one after arrival.

Short Nature Walk

Aasiaat Island is relatively low compared with many Greenland destinations, and marked hiking routes lead beyond the town into open Arctic terrain. For passengers with a longer call, a short section of one of these routes can provide coastal and archipelago views without committing to a full hike.

The established longer routes are not ideal for a typical short cruise visit. For example, the Tele Mast/Top 90 route is roughly 4.4–5 km (2.7–3.1 mi) and may require 2–4 hours, while the Nuggoq route is about 8 km (5.0 mi) and takes roughly 2–4 hours. Only attempt them when the port schedule leaves a substantial margin for the return.

Self-Guided Walking Tour

Harbour, History and Art Circuit

Distance: approximately 1.5–2 km (0.9–1.2 mi). Pure walking time: about 30–40 minutes. Recommended total time: 1.5–2 hours. Difficulty: Easy to moderate, with some gradients and uneven surfaces.

  1. Tender landing / tourist pontoon: Start in the central harbour area and take a few minutes to look across the working waterfront.
  2. Old colonial harbour: Walk through the historic cluster of traditional wooden buildings near the waterfront.
  3. Aasiaat Museum: Visit the local-history collections if the museum is open.
  4. Sod House: See the traditional turf-house reconstruction beside the museum area.
  5. Aasiaat Church: Continue uphill to the church overlooking the harbour.
  6. Assembly House: Pass the building known for its collection of Per Kirkeby paintings.
  7. Harbour and local shops: Loop back toward the waterfront, passing the commercial centre and Brættet, the traditional local provisions market area.
  8. Tender landing: Return directly to the harbour with plenty of time before the final tender.

This route keeps you close to the ship throughout and can easily be shortened if tender operations or weather reduce your time ashore.

When an Excursion Is the Better Choice

Choose an organized excursion if your priority is whale watching, iceberg sailing, kayaking or reaching the more remote parts of Aasiaat Island. These experiences depend on boats, local equipment or route knowledge and can consume a large proportion of a short port call.

Long-distance day trips to other Disko Bay towns or settlements are generally unsuitable for a normal cruise stop because scheduled local boats are not designed around cruise passengers' return times.

Practical Tips

  • Wear layers and carry windproof and waterproof outerwear. Conditions can change quickly even during summer.
  • Use sturdy footwear. Central streets are manageable, but slopes, gravel and uneven surfaces are common.
  • Do not approach or pet Greenlandic sled dogs, particularly dogs tethered in designated dog areas.
  • Public toilet facilities in town are limited. It is sensible to use the facilities on the ship before going ashore.
  • For independent boat tours, confirm the departure point, duration and cancellation arrangements before committing.
  • Tendering takes additional time in both directions. Be back at the designated landing point well before the ship's final tender rather than treating departure time as your return deadline.
